reading.synopsis: Six astronauts crash-land back on Earth after a Mars expedition, jubilant to be home, only to find every town they pass through emptying in silent terror at the sight of them. FBI agents arrive and calmly explain the truth: this crew's actual ship exploded on Mars, killing all six; a robot scavenger team recovered the corpses, so whatever has just landed cannot be the real crew. Without hesitation, the agents incinerate all six men with napalm. The story then reveals this is routine, repeating every couple of months as some unknown intelligence near Mars keeps sending duplicate 'crews' back to Earth, always destroyed on sight; a younger agent, Wilks, is left wondering aloud whether anyone has ever actually attempted to communicate with whatever these arrivals are, since anything so thoroughly convinced of its own humanity might, given the chance, become human in truth. The question is immediately foreclosed: a burned, bewildered survivor approaches him, and though it opens its mouth to speak, Wilks shoots it dead on reflex before it can say a word. The story then loops back to its opening image — a new ship crash-lands, a new set of identical astronauts climb out euphoric to be 'home' — closing on the unstated certainty that the entire cycle will simply repeat.

structure.form: short story in three movements, structured as a repeating loop: the arrival and jubilation, the reveal and execution, the coda that restarts the cycle
movements: The astronauts crash-land, celebrate their survival, and are met with inexplicable terror rather than welcome as they walk toward town.

FBI agents reveal that the real crew died on Mars and calmly execute this and all such 'duplicate' landings by napalm, a process now in its twenty-first or twenty-second iteration; agent Wilks alone questions whether real contact has ever been attempted.

A surviving, injured duplicate approaches Wilks with what looks like an attempt to communicate; he shoots it out of trained reflex before it can speak, and the story restarts with a new, identical crash-landing.
structure.point_of_view: third person, moving from the astronauts' subjective jubilation at 'returning' to Scanlan and Wilks's procedural, then troubled, perspective on the killings, so the reader experiences both the innocence of the arrivals and the moral cost paid by those ordered to destroy them.
structure.central_device: A cyclical, repeating first-contact scenario in which the visiting intelligence's method of approach — perfectly, sincerely believing itself to be the returning human crew — is treated by the receiving humans as self-evident proof of hostile intent rather than as the desperate, uncomprehending communication attempt Wilks alone suspects it might be.

characters.name: Captain Stone, Barton, Leon, Parkhurst, Vecchi, Merriweather
characters.note: Written with full, sympathetic interiority — homesickness, thoughts of wives and children, plans for reunion — right up until their deaths, so the reader's emotional identification is total before the reveal recontextualizes them as something else entirely, or perhaps not.

characters.name: Scanlan
characters.note: Entirely procedural and resigned, treating mass incineration as routine pest control; his only uncertainty is tactical (how many landed this time), never moral.

characters.name: Wilks
characters.note: The story's moral center and its only voice of doubt — he explicitly wonders whether something that behaves so convincingly human might, given contact rather than immediate violence, actually become human, but shoots the one specimen who might have tested that theory anyway, out of trained fear rather than considered judgment.

settings.name: A small California peninsula town near San Francisco (Burlingame)
settings.note: Ordinary, specific, and mapped with real place-names, which sharpens rather than softens the horror of its practiced, silent evacuation and subsequent violence.

settings.name: The cycle itself
settings.note: The story's true setting is temporal rather than geographic — an unspecified number of prior, identical iterations of this exact scenario, of which the reader witnesses only the twenty-first or twenty-second.

motifs: A returning astronaut crew whose sincere, detailed homesickness and joy is never revealed as performance or deception, leaving their exact nature genuinely uncertain
State violence executed as unremarkable routine procedure rather than as a decision requiring justification each time
A single dissenting voice (Wilks) whose doubt changes nothing and is itself overridden by trained reflex at the critical moment
A closing return to the story's opening image, structurally enacting the same endless repetition its plot describes
An entity given the chance to speak and denied it at the exact moment of possible communication
reading.significance: The story's power lies in withholding the one piece of information that would resolve its central ambiguity: what these arrivals actually are, and whether the alien intelligence sending them is malicious, uncomprehending, or simply trying, over and over, in the only way it knows how, to bring its 'crew' home. Wilks's unanswered question — 'if they... feel human, might they not become human, in time?' — is the story's clearest statement of a recurring Dick concern with what actually constitutes personhood, addressed here not through an android or replicant but through something that might be an alien's best, and most tragically misunderstood, attempt at exactly that. The story never allows either reading (malevolent infiltration vs. desperate imitation reaching for something real) to win outright, and its closing loop suggests the humans will never let themselves find out which is true.
reading.closing_note: The story's final line repeats its opening beat nearly verbatim — a new crash, a new jubilant 'We're back!' — collapsing the distinction between this iteration and the next, and confirming that nothing learned by Wilks will interrupt the cycle.

distinctive_terms.label: Bureau
distinctive_terms.note: The FBI's procedural, bureaucratic language for its recurring executions is the story's chief source of horror — routine paperwork applied to mass killing.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a recurring, unresolved first-contact scenario in which the visiting intelligence's true nature and intent are never established, only assumed and acted on with lethal force
Wilks's explicit, unresolved question of whether something that convincingly feels and behaves as human might, given the chance, actually become human

pkd_on_this_work.summary: A letter to editor Anthony Boucher documents the story's revision history, including a detail not present in the published text: an early draft apparently involved 'the time travel angle,' since removed or replaced.

evidence.source: The Selected Letters of Philip K. Dick (Volume 1)
evidence.quote: It may be that the time travel angle didn't convince you, in which case I'm sure another resolution can be found.
evidence.reading: This April 1954 letter shows the story went through at least one substantial rewrite at Boucher's request before publication, and that an earlier version turned on 'the time travel angle' — a plot mechanism absent from the alien-duplication premise of the published story, suggesting the published ending (repeating cycle, ambiguous alien mimicry) may be a later replacement for a different original resolution.

open_questions: What was the original 'time travel angle' mentioned in Dick's letter to Boucher, and how would it have changed the story's ending and meaning?
Is there a documented final exchange confirming what specific changes Boucher requested and received before publication?

Is there secondary criticism connecting this story's ambiguous, sympathetic 'duplicate' astronauts to Dick's later android and replicant fiction, given how directly Wilks's question anticipates the central concerns of Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
